questions.question: should I treat my boots out of box ? Annnnd how often should I treat them ?

hybrid.answer:
It depends on the boot. Pretreated, finished, oiled leather doesn't need treating out of the box, but distressed or rustic leather does. This is based on my Blundstones, so I can't speak for other brands.

**Out of the box**
- Most Blundstones come pretreated, and Blundstone itself doesn't recommend treating them out of the box [1].
- Rustic Brown, Crazy Horse and rustic black styles don't carry the same pretreatment as finished, oiled leather [2]. I recommend conditioning those, and I don't recommend leaving them dry, even if you bought them for that look [3].

**How often**
- I do it when I feel they need it, and I probably do it too little. It depends on how much you wear them and where you go [4].
- I'd treat them when the leather looks or feels dry, or when water stops beading on top. Clean them regularly too, because dirt wears the leather down faster [5].
- I used to say you may have to wax them every month, or even every week if you're very hard on them [6]. Anything leather that hasn't been conditioned in a few months should definitely get conditioned [7].

questions.question: So if I buy the levis 501 shrink to fit will they get tighter after washing?

hybrid.answer:
Yes. Shrink-to-fit 501s shrink the first time you soak or wash them, mostly in the waist, and then loosen up again with wear. In my videos, putting them in the bathtub is what shrinks them [1]. That's why I'd go two sizes up in the waist [1].

**How much they shrink**
- After I shrank mine, they came out smaller than regular rinsed 501s [2].
- The shrinking showed up mainly in the waist. The length barely changed [3][4].
- The waist was tight enough that it was hard to get comfortable at first. I went with a 29 waist and could barely pull them on [5].

**Heat and the dryer matter**
- If you don't use very hot water and don't put them in the dryer, you get a really nice fit [6].
- A hot wash and the dryer make them shrink more [6].

**They stretch back out**
- With frequent wear I expect them to stretch to about the same size as a rinsed pair [7].
- A week later the waist and thighs had stretched enough that I could wear a belt [8].
- After about a year, mine fit really well [5].

questions.question: I'm usually a 33x30 in Levi's 502s, what size should I buy in these? [501 STF]

hybrid.answer:
By my rule, a 33x30 in your usual size becomes a 35 waist and a 32 length in 501 STF: two sizes up in the waist and two inches longer. Treat that as my rule applied to your numbers, since I haven't compared 502s to 501s. I also haven't said whether a 35 waist is made.

- **Waist:** I usually go two sizes up in STF 501s [1]. The jeans shrink down when you soak them, so sizing up doesn't leave them too big [2].
- **Length:** Levi's recommends two inches longer than you'd normally wear, and I think they're right [3]. After you get them wet, the jeans fit like regular jeans [3].
- **My own experience:** I first ignored Levi's advice and bought closer to my normal size, since I'd read the waist stretches a lot [4]. Later I realized I'd made a mistake and that sizing up two is correct [3].
- **Check on my own pair:** I went up two sizes, from 30 to 32, and the waist doesn't correlate to the tag size, which is why you size up [2].

questions.question: Why do you cuff your jeans?

hybrid.answer:
I cuff mainly because I can't settle on a hem length. I can never decide between no break, half break or full break, and cuffing is the only solution I've found for that [1]. Cuffing is also how I deal with jeans that run long or wide. With my 501s, I'd have gotten a 32 length, but I cuffed them because my current style doesn't suit wider-legged pants left uncuffed [2]. Length matters most to me, because if jeans look too long they just look bad [3].

I've also said I used to cuff my jeans all the time, but now I like them worn down over my boots [4].

questions.question: So do you prefer [the Red Wing 3335s] over the 1907s?

hybrid.answer:
I used to say yes, but now I'm less sure. I'm on record saying the 3335s are my favorite Red Wings of all time, and they still might be, but probably not. I like the 875s, 1907s and Iron Rangers for their own characteristics [1]. I also like the 3335s because they're stitch-down, lighter and easier to walk or lightly hike in. Even so, they were on the list of boots I'm getting rid of [1].

**Why I preferred the 3335s:** They were my favorite boots I've ever had, ahead of the 1907s and 875s, and a dramatically better all-around boot for hikes and walks in the woods [2]. They have a Vibram mini lug sole that I expect to hold up better than the crepe soles on the 875s and 1907s [3]. I was still calling them my favorite Red Wings in early 2023 [4].

**Where the 1907s win:** The 1907s and 875s are more beefily constructed, so if you need a tough boot, the 3335s are probably not the ones to go for [2]. In my opinion the 1907s are Red Wing's best heritage boots by far, and I'd pick them if you're looking at a moc toe Red Wing [5].

questions.question: How does the made in England boot stack up to Solovairs? [Dr. Martens]

hybrid.answer:
I think Solovair is the better boot and it costs less, so I'd pick it over the made in England Dr. Martens [1]. You get a better boot for about $40 less, with none of the Dr. Martens markup [2].

**Where Solovair wins**
- The outsole is heavier, and the midsole is a thicker, more robust felted one [3][4].
- Solovair uses full grain leather on certain models [5]. The 8-eye Derby has waxed full grain leather, which gives weather resistance without flaking [6]. Not every Solovair is full grain, and some Dr. Martens are, so check the specific model [7].
- Solovair boots have a shank, so they're more comfortable over long periods. They're also welted in a more widely accepted way, so they're easier to resole [8].
- Solovair sells replacement soles on its website, which is why I think its boots will last much longer [9].

**Where Dr. Martens holds up**
- The made in England leather and midsoles are probably on par with Solovair [10].
- If the yellow stitching matters to you, you have to go Dr. Martens [11].
- On value alone, I'd say the made in England pair is probably not worth the extra $90 over the Thailand-made pair. It's for big Dr. Martens fans [12].

**Solovair downsides**
- My first pair had a back tab rip off within a week of wear [13].
- Sizing can be off. My Derbys came out like clown shoes, so consider sizing down a half size [14].

questions.question: Hi, I am going on a 4 day hike and I am wondering if I can use my blundstone for them, what do you think?

hybrid.answer:
I wouldn't make them my first pick for a 4-day hike, mainly because they lack ankle support. Apparently they aren't good boots for mountaineering for that reason [1]. They did hold up well on hikes and mountain climbs in Maine, though I only scuffed them up a little [1]. I haven't tested them on a multi-day hike, so I can't say how they'd do over four days.

- **Break-in:** Make sure they're fully broken in first. I got big blisters when I started running and walking the track in them, and they stopped after two to three weeks [2].
- **Water:** They're water resistant, not waterproof. You can get them wet, but don't go swimming in them because water will come in [3].

questions.question: I'm 5'11-225 lbs with a dad bod. What's the most cost efficient and quality t shirt for me? Also, what size would u prefer?

hybrid.answer:
I'd go for the Muji t-shirt. Uniqlo is the best deal if you're smaller, but I say to pick Muji if you're taller or wider [1]. It costs about $4 or $5 more than Uniqlo's $20 shirt, but it's significantly longer and a good deal wider, which suits a bigger guy [2]. Earlier, I found Muji's extra cost justified because it feels better, with a slightly thicker, tighter collar [3].

**Size:** I haven't covered a specific size for your height and weight. What I can say is that Muji is cut longer and wider, so it already gives you room and it's slightly tented out, which you'd probably like if you're a little bigger [2]. In my own fit preferences, I like a lot of space across the shoulders and shirts that flatten me out [4].

**Other options:**
- **Uniqlo:** At $20 it's probably the best shirt for the price bar none, but it's a starter tee, and you want Muji if you're taller or wider [5][1].
- **Los Angeles Apparel:** It's very large and fits me like a tent [6], but I think it might win if you size down one [7].
- **House of Blanks:** At $35, made in Canada, it has zero torque and is an outstanding value [8].

questions.question: Hi, what are some fall/winter sneakers you'd recommend?

hybrid.answer:
The Samara is the one I'd point you to for fall and winter. It's the sneaker I made with Goral Footwear, so it's my own collaboration, and I call it my favorite hiking shoe around [1]. It's meant to look just as good in town as in the woods [2].

- **Why it suits cold, wet weather:** The outsole is Vibram Arctic Grip, which is meant to increase slip resistance on wet ice [3]. The lug also turns blue when temperatures fall below freezing, to warn you of ice formation [4].
- **Feit Classic Low:** These are my favorite sneakers and I wear them every day [5]. I haven't said they're specifically a fall/winter pick.
- **New Balance 990 V6:** I highly recommend it as a lifestyle and walking shoe [6]. I haven't singled it out for cold weather either.

I haven't done a broader roundup of cold-weather sneakers, so the Samara is the only one I've covered with winter conditions in mind.

questions.question: 1907 vs the 875's? What's the difference?

hybrid.answer:
I'd get the 1907 over the 875 if you're choosing a Red Wing moc toe [1]. The 1907 costs about $10 more, and for that you get a storm welt, a removable leather footbed and leather laces [2].

- **Storm welt:** The 1907 has a storm (Norwegian-style) welt. It removes the small channel where water can get in, so water runs off like a gutter [3]. I find that invaluable [4].
- **Footbed:** The 1907 comes with Red Wing's removable leather footbed, which typically costs $40 separately [4]. You can pull it out at the end of the day so the boots dry faster [4].
- **Laces:** It comes with leather laces, which are typically $15 [5].
- **Price:** The 1907 is $10 more, and the extras more than cover that [2][5].
- **Soles:** Both have crepe soles [6], and I don't really like those [7].

**Water:** In my waterproof test, one 1907 leaked almost immediately through the stitching and the other stayed dry [8]. I'd still expect them to hold up fine in rain, grass or mud [8]. Leather welted boots in general aren't great for water resistance [9].

questions.question: How does Uniqlo compare to The Front General Store,  Proclub, and Hanes? ie what is the best budget shirt?

hybrid.answer:
For the best budget shirt on price, I'd go with Uniqlo. At about $20 it's probably the best t-shirt you can get for the money [1]. If you'll spend a bit more for a Japan-made shirt with more character, Front General Store is the step up.

**Uniqlo:** It's a rough, open-end starter tee [2]. You get a bound neck collar, so it doesn't wiggle [3]. I gave its heavyweight crew the best value heavyweight or all-around award [4].

**Front General Store:** It's a $40, 100% Japan-made shirt with great proportions and feel [5]. It's one of the best shirts you can get under about $40 [6]. I rated its softness 6 out of 10 [6]. When I picked a favorite in the best-value category, I went with it that day, over House of Blanks [7].

**Pro Club:** I like it, but it's the roughest shirt in that group [8]. I rated its softness 4 out of 10 [8].

**Hanes:** It's a classic $10 great shirt [9]. I rated its softness 7 out of 10 [9].

So Uniqlo is the best value overall. Hanes is the cheapest and softer than Pro Club. Pro Club is the roughest and most old-school. Front General Store is the one to pick if you want something nicer than a starter tee.

questions.question: Would you recommend this [Barbour Bedale] or the flint and tinder for someone who would use it like a rain jacket but also a windbreaker and a spring light jacket?

hybrid.answer:
I'd lean toward the Barbour Bedale for rain, and the Flint and Tinder is the easier all-round pick for the spring-jacket side. I haven't tested the Flint and Tinder in the rain, and I haven't covered wind resistance for either one, so that part isn't covered.

**Barbour Bedale**
- A new Bedale with fresh wax didn't leak at all in my shower test [1]. It's very water-resistant when properly treated, though not truly waterproof [2].
- It has rain features I like: a storm flap behind the zipper so water won't run through it [3], and storm cuffs that help in bad weather [4]. I also highly suggest getting the hood, since without it the jacket only suits milder days [5].
- It's not a designated rain jacket. The 6 oz fabric is lightweight, so you can wear it any time of year [6].
- The catch is that patina and water resistance trade off. As the wax wears away, you get the look but lose some practicality [7].

**Flint and Tinder Waxed Trucker**
- I say it's for everyone, because it's cut well, lined, and goes with anything [8]. It's a lighter weight, so it's comfortable, and it's not crazy lightweight [9].
- At $300 it's made in the US with no obvious sacrifice, which is why it's hard not to recommend [10]. That praise came in a sponsored segment, though I'd talked about the jacket before the sponsorship.

If rain is the first job, I'd pick the Bedale and buy the hood with it. If you mostly want a light spring layer that only sometimes sees rain, the Flint and Tinder fits that well.

questions.question: Great video. But just curious, how can you say it's a con that the Huckberry jacket is unlined when they sell two different versions of lined waxed truckers: wool, and flannel?

hybrid.answer:
The unlined con applies only to the unlined version I tested in that video, not to the lined Huckberry versions you mention. That jacket was the cheapest, simplest, unlined basic one on the list [1]. My con was that I always prefer a lining on a waxed jacket, so the wax isn't touching your clothes or arms [2]. Huckberry does sell an unlined version alongside the lined one [3].

The lined versions are a different story:
- **Flannel-lined:** I describe the standard Flint and Tinder trucker as lined, so it's comfortable and you don't get wax on your skin [4].
- **Wool-lined:** There is a wool-lined version, though it comes in much more limited quantity [5]. I haven't got one yet, and I know it's heavier all around [6].

My view on linings has softened a bit. I still usually want a liner, but I now see why you might leave one out. A satin-sleeve lining can limit how often you can wear the jacket once it gets warm [7].
